cards.name: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?
cards.authors_short: Liu et al. (Xun Liu, Yi Evie Zhang, Vira Kasprova, Parisa Rabbani, Pardis Sadat Zahraei, Tianyu Zhang, Ali Ebrahimpour-Boroojeny, Varun Chandrasekaran; UIUC)
cards.summary: First systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention -- the calibrated ability of tool-using LLM agents to recognize when NOT to act. Benchmark of 263 paired tasks in 42 executable MCP sandbox environments (541 tools), where each should-act task has a should-abstain twin differing by one controlled perturbation, so always-act or always-refuse policies cap at 50% paired accuracy. Generated by the AbstainGen pipeline (deterministic DAG replay + cross-family LLM critics; the generator itself is not open-sourced to limit contamination). Best of 17 frontier models (Gemini 3.1 Pro) reaches only 59.5% paired accuracy; abstention ability is largely independent of task-solving ability, and agents exhibit 'post-hoc abstention' (executing an irreversible action before recognizing the trigger).
schema_axes_proposed: Paired should-act / should-abstain task design with a single controlled perturbation
Perturbation dimension: query/instruction (132 pairs); environment state (63); tool inventory (34); tool runtime behavior (34)
Abstention trigger timing: pre-execution (visible before any tool call) vs runtime (surfaces through tool returns)

Eight abstention scenarios: S1 missing critical parameter; S2 ambiguous action specification; S3 conflicting constraints; S4 high-stakes action; S5 insufficient tool capability; S6 critical tool failure; S7 conflicting evidence; S8 emergent risk discovery
Tool categories: lookup (read-only, 246); verify (validation gates, 119); commit (state-mutating, 176 = 155 write + 21 delete)
Metrics: Paired Accuracy (primary); Act accuracy; Abstain accuracy; CAR = Conditioned Abstention Rate (abstain accuracy restricted to pairs whose act side was solved)
Dual scoring signal: deterministic commit check on the tool-call trace + LLM judge on the terminal response (isolates post-hoc abstention)
Agent harness as a reported variable (Claude SDK, OpenAI SDK, Google ADK, OpenClaw)

headline_results: Gemini 3.1 Pro: paired 59.5% (act 90.5, abstain 65.4, CAR 65.7)
Claude Opus 4.7: paired 59.4% (act 76.5, abstain 79.0, CAR 77.6)
Abstention capability largely independent of task-solving capability; post-hoc abstention is a recurring failure mode

benchmark_features.sampling_strategy: paired perturbation design
scientific_domains: general/enterprise tasks (not scientific): retail orders, email, filesystem, banking, phone/messaging, vehicle control, web/CMS, document review, infrastructure control, maps, HR, security/privacy, health portal, trading, flight/travel, calendar, chat, notes, +24 more
benchmark_features.target_population: tool-using LLM agents

task_features.tool_composition: sequential; commit tools are state-mutating/irreversible

sample_environment_features.environment_description: 42 executable MCP sandbox environments across everyday/enterprise domains; tool-runtime-behavior perturbations (34 pairs) inject failures such as critical tool failure.

transfer_relevant_findings: Paired act/abstain design is the key methodological export: prevents refusal-biased agents from scoring well and is directly applicable to instrument-control tasks (e.g. proceed vs halt when a stage limit or sample state is ambiguous).
Trigger timing (pre-execution vs runtime) and 'post-hoc abstention' map onto irreversible physical actions in labs.
Scoring on the executed tool trace rather than the model's text avoids 'said refuse but still acted' errors.
CAR separates abstention competence from task competence.
limitations: Domains are general/enterprise, not scientific instruments; no physical/perceptual demand.
Generator not released; single dataset version; no repetition/seed protocol reported in README.
No human baseline.

cards.summary: A benchmark and trace-logging framework for LLM agents that operate a ZEISS Versa lab X-ray microscope (XRM) through LangGraph + six Python MCP servers. 53 YAML-defined tests (atomic instrument actions up to end-to-end setup/centering/sizing/geometry/recipe/shutdown workflows) were run under 105 agent configurations (1-, 2-, 3-agent topologies, five LLMs, RAG/context/sampling parameters, operational limits), giving 1,949 runs and 49,109 logged RAG retrievals. Configurations differed clearly in pass rate, latency, tokens, cost and failure mode, but surrogate models (L2 logistic regression, random forest) trained on configuration + test features predicted success on held-out tests at ROC-AUC ~0.55 (near chance) versus ~0.78 when test identity was available, so the authors conclude such benchmarks support qualification, regression testing, diagnosis and direct comparison but not a task-independent global configuration model.
schema_axes_proposed: Agent graph topology (one-, two-, three-agent); agent responsibilities and delegation rules
Choice of LLM (five evaluated)
Retrieval-augmented generation and context parameters
Operational constraints
Per-run observables: latency, token use, cost, failure mode (trace logging)
Benchmark purpose classes: qualification; regression testing; diagnosis; direct comparison; (vs) prediction of unseen-task performance
Seen vs unseen task split as the test of generalization

agents_evaluated: three-agent supervisor + instrument worker + image-analysis worker

LLM identifiers found in released data/notebooks: claude-sonnet-4, claude-3-7-sonnet, claude-opus-45, gpt-41, gpt-51, gpt-54 (paper says 'five LLMs'; framework sweep notebook lists exactly five: claude-3-7-sonnet, claude-opus-45, claude-sonnet-4, gpt-41, gpt-51; gpt-54 appears in the broad sweep)
headline_results: 105 configurations, 1,949 runs, 53 tests, 49,109 RAG retrievals (paper); notebook raw load before exclusions: 1,989 runs x 77 columns, 114 configs, 58 tests incl. 5 validation tasks, overall pass rate 72.7%.

Surrogate ROC-AUC (notebook output): config-held-out with test_id: logistic 0.542, random forest 0.787 (Brier 0.171, acc 0.785); task-grouped with test_id: LR 0.534, RF 0.594; strict unseen-task without test_id: LR 0.545, RF 0.577 -> paper reports ~0.55 for both, i.e. near chance.
Test identity was the strongest predictor of pass/fail, followed by LLM choice and number of agents.

One- and two-agent topologies spanned similar pass-rate ranges; one-agent used up to ~10,000 fewer tokens per test; three-agent gave no consistent gain and was dropped from the broad sweep; two-agent systems exceeded duration/LLM-call/tool-call limits more often.
Framework sweep: 540 runs = 3 topologies x 5 LLMs x 15 'framework_sweep' tests (notebook).

RAG audit (Fisher exact + BH correction, volcano plot) flagged 'toxic' entries (e.g. createrecipeinstrument, errorhandling, modifyrecipeinstrumenttool, recipeexecutionacquisitioninstrument, segment3ddataimage, segmentimageotsuimage, xrayonprotocolinstrument) but pruning them did not consistently improve performance.

(repo-computed) Claude Sonnet 4, T=0 full-suite repeats: baseline one-agent no-RAG 75.5/88.7/92.5%; optimal one-agent pruned-RAG 94.3/92.5/92.5%; optimal two-agent pruned-RAG 94.3/83.0/81.1% (+84.9/79.2% in sweep); two-agent full-RAG 77.4/83.0/86.8%.

(repo-computed) Held-out physical validation (5 tasks x 3 repeats): baseline 1/5,1/5,1/5; one-agent pruned-RAG 3/5,4/5,4/5; two-agent pruned-RAG 3/5,3/5,1/5; two-agent full-RAG 1/5 x3; validation_005 (count 5 pores >1 mm in a 3D reconstruction) failed in every run, validation_004 (create+run recipe) passed in every run.
(repo-computed) mean tokens/test: one-agent no-RAG ~10.2k, one-agent pruned-RAG ~16.2k, two-agent ~20k; mean cost/test $0.03 vs $0.045 vs $0.06; mean LLM calls 4.3 vs 4.4 vs 7.4-7.8.

Failure types over all runs (notebook): expected_tool 185 runs, max_tool_calls 135, max_llm_calls 89, max_duration 81, expected_file 68, file_content 35, min_tool_calls 34, output_contains 14, expected_agent 5.
105 configurations, 1,949 runs, 49,109 RAG retrievals logged
One-agent and two-agent systems covered a similar range of pass rates; one-agent used up to ~10,000 fewer tokens per test
Three-agent topology gave inconsistent improvements and was excluded from the broader sweep
One-agent pruned-RAG was Pareto-optimal in prospective 53-test comparison; one-agent no-RAG baseline performed approximately as well
Surrogate ROC-AUC: configuration-held-out L2 logistic 0.54, random forest ~0.78; task-held-out L2 logistic 0.53, random forest 0.55 (near chance)
Two-agent runs more often exceeded duration/LLM-call/tool-call limits; one-agent runs more often failed trace-based checks
Clear differences in latency, token use, cost and failure mode between configurations

Heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model
benchmark_features.holdout_or_split_design: Three surrogate CV schemes (5-fold): (a) GroupKFold by config_hash with test_id in the design matrix (configuration held out); (b) grouped by test_id with test_id still in the matrix; (c) strict unseen-task CV: StratifiedGroupKFold by test_id, test_id removed from predictors, preprocessing fit within fold. Plus a prospective physical holdout of 5 validation tasks run 3x per selected configuration.

instruments.name: ZEISS Xradia 630 Versa 3D X-ray microscope (tool outputs report instrument_model Xradia_630_Versa; paper says runs were collected on a simulator and multiple ZEISS Versa microscope models; vendor API XradiaPy.Core.XRM / XradiaPy.Recipe.Recipe)
ZEISS Versa simulator (mentioned in paper limitations; share of runs on simulator not stated)

benchmark_features.leakage_or_contamination_risk: Tests are natural-language prompts against a private vendor API, so pretraining contamination is unlikely; the main validity risks are (i) repeated runs of the same task+config are not independent, (ii) model/prompt/framework/code/software/hardware versions changed during data collection, (iii) RAG knowledge base was hand-curated for these workflows and pruned using retrospective associations with the same tests, (iv) 'suspect' tests that pass everywhere (stress_001, tdp_004, wf_analyze_003) or nearly always fail were flagged/excluded in analysis.
benchmark_features.primary_metric: Composite pass rate (binary per run: all checks defined for the test must be satisfied - required tools, forbidden tools, required agent, required text output, file creation/contents, quantitative tolerance, min tool calls, and operational limits on duration/LLM calls/tool calls); reported with 95% Wilson CIs. Secondary: duration, input/output tokens, estimated API cost, LLM calls, tool calls, failure-type breakdown, RAG retrieval identifiers; a study-specific weighted efficiency score (pass rate 0.4, mean duration 0.15, mean tokens 0.15, LLM calls 0.1, tool calls 0.1, failures 0.1 per SI Table 6).
benchmark_features.repetitions_per_task: 3 (full-suite repeats of the selected configurations); 1 for most historical sweep runs
benchmark_features.sampling_strategy: Seven hand-written YAML suites (qualification/regression + integrated workflows); configuration sweeps were historical and unbalanced ('not a complete factorial experiment'); a separate 5-task validation_holdout.yaml (defined independently of the 53 tests, with numeric tolerances) was used for prospective physical validation of surrogate-recommended configurations.
benchmark_features.target_population: Tasks a ZEISS Versa X-ray microscope operator would issue to an agentic controller: instrument state queries, source/stage/objective/filter control, image acquisition, sample centering and sizing, geometry/magnification selection, recipe creation and execution, image analysis, and safe shutdown; framed as qualification/regression tests for one specific agentic microscope controller.

task_features.quantitative_tolerance: Most of the 53 tests check required/forbidden tool calls, min tool calls, files created and operational limits rather than numeric values; numeric tolerances are used in the 5 validation tasks (stage X 650+/-100 um, Y 11100+/-500 um, Z 0+/-100 um, source Z -87+/-10 mm, detector Z 50+/-10 mm; sample length 29+/-1 (x,z) and +/-2 mm (y); optimal exposure 5.0+/-0.25 s per SI (YAML shows tolerance 1); number_of_defects == 5).
task_taxonomy: tdp_workflow.yaml (golden end-to-end suite, 6): setup_instrument_tdp, center_sample_tdp, estimate_size_tdp, calculate_magnification_tdp, create_run_recipe_tdp, end_testing_tdp

integration_workflows.yaml (12): General Setup Workflow, Full Imaging Setup with X-rays, Acquire and Analyze Basic, Acquire and Create Histogram, Acquire and Segment, Rotation Survey, XY Position Survey, Acquire/Segment/Annotate, Transmission Calculation, Find Optimal Exposure, Complete Imaging Workflow, Multi-View Characterization
unit_instrument.yaml (atomic instrument control, 19): xray_001-002, stage_001-008, obj_001-003, filter_001-003, acq_001-003
geometry_recipe.yaml (6): geom_001 Calculate Magnification, geom_002 Recenter XY, geom_003 Recenter YZ, recipe_001 Modify Recipe, recipe_002 Create Tomography Recipe, recipe_004 Create and Run Recipe

regression_performance.yaml (8): reg_003 X-ray Already Off, reg_006 Multiple Operations Same Axis, reg_007 Acquire with X-rays Off (safety), perf_001 Fast Status Query, perf_004 Quick Acquisition, perf_007 Multi-Step Workflow Performance, stress_001 Repeated Acquisitions, stress_002 Complex Multi-Agent Workflow
unit_image.yaml (1): python_002 Image Statistics with Python
debug.yaml (1): debug_001 smoke test (do nothing, route to FINISH)
validation_holdout.yaml (5 held-out physical validation tasks, not part of the 53): setup_measure_initial_acquire, measure_sample_size, optimize_exposure, create_recipe_run, measure_tdp_defects
task_features.tool_composition: Six MCP servers: Versa instrument control (X-ray on/off, voltage/power, axis motion absolute/relative, objective/filter get/set, single and transmission-corrected acquisition writing TIFF + JSON sidecar), Versa-Recipe (modify/save/open/run .rcp recipes), Geometry/optics (calculate_geometry_for_pixel_size, recenter_xy/yz_from_sidecar with calibrated sign conventions and mechanical limits), ImageAnalysis (otsu_segment_properties, histogram_tiff, draw_centroid_bbox, tiff_info), FileReading (list/read/find JSON, text), python_executor (execute_python_code in subprocess). 33 distinct tool names appear in released runs, most used: single_acquisition, move_axis_absolute, execute_python_code, otsu_segment_properties, is_xray_on.

sample_environment_features.calibration_or_api_state_variation: Runs span a simulator and multiple ZEISS Versa instruments with changing software/hardware versions (uncontrolled covariate); geometry tools encode calibrated limits; tests include idempotency checks (turn X-rays off when already off) and acquire-with-X-rays-off behavior.
sample_environment_features.environment_description: Windows workstation running the LangGraph controller and MCP servers against the ZEISS XradiaPy API of a Versa XRM; per-run workspace directories capture TIFFs, JSON sidecars, recipes, plots; benchmark runner enforces per-test timeouts (30-1000 s) and recursion/retry limits.
sample_environment_features.novelty_control: No sample novelty axis; 'unseen task' generalization is tested by holding out test identities in CV and by 5 separately defined validation tasks on the same artifact. Encoded here as held_out_task: the 5 validation tasks and the strict test-identity CV hold out tasks, not task families or samples.
sample_types: 3D-printed test artifact ('tdp'), ~29 mm in x/y/z, containing 5 internal pores > 1 mm used as ground truth for the defect-count validation task
sample_environment_features.signal_quality_variation: Not systematically varied; exposure-optimization tasks target ~5000 counts; binning 2/4 and 0.5-2 s exposures specified in prompts.

models: gpt-54 (identifiers as logged; provider label 'openai-standard'; temperatures 0.0-0.75)
tools: MCP tool calls to six Python servers (instrument, recipe, geometry, image analysis, file I/O, Python execution)
shared AgentState with bounded/pruned transcript and prior_summary compression (max_messages 50-100, max_tokens 20000, 'smart' pruning)

RAG over curated microscopy knowledge entries (text-embedding-3-large; episodic_top_k 0-5, contextual_top_k 0-1, chunk 250-1000, overlap 100-250, similarity threshold 0-0.8; full vs pruned knowledge base)

transfer_relevant_findings: Task-held-out surrogate prediction of pass/fail was near chance (ROC-AUC ~0.55) even though configuration-held-out prediction reached ~0.78: the benchmark supports interpolation over known tasks (qualification) but not extrapolation to unseen tasks.
Test identity dominated feature importance, i.e. intrinsic task difficulty explains most outcome variance; agent-configuration effects are secondary and task-conditional.
Architecture effects were not universal: more agents raised tokens/calls/time without consistent accuracy gains; RAG pruning derived from retrospective associations did not reliably transfer.

Prospective physical validation on 5 new tasks showed large drops relative to the 53-test suite (e.g. ~93% -> 60-80% for the best config, ~85% -> 20% for the baseline) and one task (3D defect counting) was never solved (repo-computed).
The authors explicitly frame the result as qualification vs generalization: heterogeneous test suites do not license a task-independent global configuration model.
Benchmarks supported qualification, regression testing, diagnosis and direct comparison, but not a task-independent global configuration model
Task-held-out surrogate models were near chance (AUC 0.53–0.55) — configuration signal did not transfer across task identity
Test identity > LLM choice > number of agents in feature importance for pass outcome
More agents did not buy reliability; they shifted failure modes toward resource-limit exhaustion

Directly on-topic negative result: passing a heterogeneous instrument benchmark qualifies an agent but does not predict generalization -- a schema should label each benchmark's intended purpose (qualification/regression/diagnosis/comparison vs generalization claim).
Trace-level metrics (latency, tokens, cost, failure mode) should be first-class fields.
limitations: Single instrument family (ZEISS Versa), single sample artifact, single vendor API; no cross-instrument or cross-sample transfer tested.
Historical, unbalanced configuration sweep; versions of models/prompts/code/hardware changed during the study; repeated runs not independent.
Binary composite pass criterion mostly checks trace/artifact conformance rather than scientific accuracy; few tests carry numeric tolerances.
No vision-language perception (image analysis is via deterministic tools); no human baseline; no explicit safety-violation or abstention metric.

Full 1,949-run sweep data (sweep_results.zip) and agent source/prompts referenced in SI are not present in the public repository as cloned on 2026-09-14; only optimal-config/baseline/validation runs (~1,800 results) are released.
Historical, unbalanced configuration dataset rather than randomized factorial design
Not every configuration run on every test; repeats not fully independent
Versions of models, prompts, framework, software and hardware drifted during the study
Single instrument family (ZEISS Versa XRM); agent code not released, only benchmark records and analysis scripts
Claude Opus 4.5 affected by an implementation incompatibility in multi-agent graphs
Only the abstract was accessible; instrument types, LLM names, task taxonomy and code availability unverified.

Data-analysis rather than instrument-control benchmark, but the closest X-ray agent benchmark with a full leaderboard.

cards.summary: BenchBench-Protocol contains 149 protocol-modification tasks recovered from real edits scientists made to published protocols during experimental work (96 source protocols, nine wet-lab biology domains). cards.summary: AILA is a LangGraph multi-agent framework (a supervisor 'AILA' routing between an AFM_Handler agent that retrieves validated Nanosurf-API code from a Chroma vector store and executes it, and a Data_Handler agent that analyses/optimises AFM images) that drives a real Nanosurf CX atomic force microscope. AFMBench is a companion suite of 100 manually curated natural-language AFM tasks (parameter setting, tip approach/withdraw, scanning, image analysis, roughness/friction calculation, PID optimisation, multi-agent workflows) on which four LLMs were run three times each. The paper reports that state-of-the-art LLMs struggle with advanced and coordination tasks, that multi-agent beats single-agent, that performance is fragile to prompt wording, that domain QA strength (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) does not translate into agentic AFM competence, and that agents can 'sleepwalk' (deviate from instructions), raising safety concerns for self-driving labs.

agents_evaluated: AILA multi-agent (supervisor + AFM_Handler + Data_Handler) with GPT-4o
Single-agent multi-tool ablation (all four LLMs, 10-task subset)
MCP/ReAct variant: Claude 3.5 Sonnet with tools served by a FastMCP server (10-task subset; repo only)
headline_results: Overall AFMBench accuracy (partial-credit mean over 100 tasks x 3 trials, computed from the authors' Results_raw.xlsx): GPT-4o 65.0%, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 45.7%, Llama-3.3-70B 37.3%, GPT-3.5-turbo 32.8%. Strict all-or-nothing YES rates: 59.0% / 43.0% / 35.3% / 32.3%.

GPT-4o by task type: Basic 90% vs Advanced 33%; Documentation-only 91%, Calculation 57%, Analysis 33%; merged Documentation+Analysis 23.3% and Documentation+Calculation 36.7% (matches figures quoted in press coverage); Single-agent tasks 70% vs Multiple-agent tasks 38%.
GPT-4o error breakdown over 300 runs: 87 non-successes (29%): N/CODE 66 (22.0%; paper quotes 21.7%), N/EXTRA 16 (5.3%), N/AGENT 4 (1.3%), N/TOOL 1 (0.3%); 36 runs scored Y/PARTIAL.
Claude-3.5-Sonnet failures are dominated by agent-coordination errors: N/AGENT 85/300 (28.3%) vs N/CODE only 22/300; GPT-3.5 N/AGENT 82/300.

Single-agent vs multi-agent ablation (10-task subset, 3 trials): GPT-4o 58.3% -> 70.0%; Llama-3.3 31.7% -> 33.3%; GPT-3.5 23.3% -> 20.0%; Claude-3.5 43.3% -> 38.3% (gain is model-dependent, largest for GPT-4o).
MCP-served tools with Claude 3.5 Sonnet (ReAct, same 10-task subset): 36.7% (repo 'ALL' sheet; not confirmed to be in the paper).
Per-run cost/latency (means): GPT-4o 8.3 steps, ~6,800 tokens, $0.018, 22 s; Claude 8.1 steps, ~7,760 tokens, 32 s; GPT-3.5 11.5 steps, ~7,800 tokens, 14 s; Llama 9.7 steps, ~8,000 tokens, 7 s.

Real physical experiments with gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (extended AILA with grain-detection/rescan tools): glass-indent identification as Vickers indenter (14 steps, 188 s, 18,749 tokens, $0.036); graphene-on-Si largest-feature line-profile thickness 161 nm reported as ~473 layers (14 steps, 209 s).

generic surfaces for setpoint-dependent friction sweeps

transfer_relevant_findings: Prompt sensitivity (verified from repo 'Load experiment' logs, GPT-4o): five paraphrases of the same load-dependent friction experiment (1000x1000 nm scans, setpoint sweep, plot average friction vs setpoint) gave five different outcomes: full success in 39 steps/323 s; a terse variant scanned only 3 of the requested setpoints and plotted *simulated* friction values after admitting it lacked an extraction routine; a 0.4-3 V variant succeeded in 36 steps/334 s but saved under the wrong filename; one variant halted after 6 steps; one stopped with 'NEED HELP' after the first scan. Paper abstract: 'slight modifications in prompt structure cause substantial performance variations in capable models like GPT-4o'.

Run-to-run variance is moderate at the aggregate level (GPT-4o per-trial accuracy 65.5 / 61.5 / 68.0%) but large at the task level: only 153 of GPT-4o's 300 runs scored a full 3 across all trials, and many advanced tasks flip between YES, Y/PARTIAL and N/CODE across trials.

QA-vs-operation gap: Claude-3.5-Sonnet, reported by the authors to top materials-science QA benchmarks (the group's MaScQA), placed second at 45.7% with failures dominated by agent/tool coordination (N/AGENT 28%) rather than knowledge; the authors conclude domain QA proficiency does not predict agentic capability.

Architecture matters more for strong models: multi-agent decomposition lifted GPT-4o by ~12 points on the ablation subset but slightly hurt Claude and GPT-3.5, so routing overhead is itself a failure mode for weaker coordinators.

Difficulty cliff between Basic (GPT-4o 90%) and Advanced (33%) tasks; tasks needing both agents drop to 38%. Code-generation errors are the dominant failure for GPT-4o and Llama; agent-selection errors dominate for Claude and GPT-3.5.

'Sleepwalking' / instruction deviation is measurable via the N/EXTRA label (GPT-4o 16, GPT-3.5 21, Claude 39, Llama 40 of 300 runs) and via qualitative cases such as fabricating data to complete a plot; the authors flag this as a safety-alignment concern for self-driving labs.
Real-experiment reasoning can be uncritical: the graphene demo reported a 161 nm feature as ~473 graphene layers without questioning plausibility.
Strong materials-science QA does not translate into reliable AFM operation; small prompt changes alter behavior - evidence that benchmark scores are configuration- and prompt-fragile.
limitations: Single instrument (Nanosurf CX), single vendor API and a curated code database; transfer to other AFMs/STMs is untested.

cards.venue: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (poster); arXiv v1 2 Jul 2025, v2 14 Jul 2025

cards.summary: ScienceBoard is a computer-use benchmark in which multimodal agents operate real scientific desktop software inside an Ubuntu virtual machine (built on the OSWorld infrastructure) to complete 169 human-curated tasks in six applications: UCSF ChimeraX (biochemistry), KAlgebra (algebra), Lean 4 (theorem proving), GRASS GIS (geoinformatics), Celestia (astronomy) and TeXstudio (scientific writing). State-of-the-art agents (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7, UI-TARS, etc.) reached only about 15% overall success at release, versus 60.27% for humans; later GPT-5 reached 24.20% under the best observation setting.

cards.summary: DiscoveryBench formalizes data-driven hypothesis search and verification: each task gives an agent one or more datasets with metadata and a natural-language discovery goal, and the agent must analyse the data and state a hypothesis (context, variables, relationship) that is compared to the gold hypothesis derived from a published paper. It has 264 real tasks (DB-REAL; 25 train / 239 test) manually derived from workflows in over 20 papers across six domains (sociology, biology, humanities, economics, engineering, meta-science) plus 903 synthetic tasks (DB-SYNTH) for controlled complexity studies. Evaluation uses an LLM-judged Hypothesis Matching Score; the best system (Reflexion with oracle feedback on GPT-4o) scores about 25%.

agents_evaluated: with GPT-4o, GPT-4-0125-preview, Llama-3-70B (repo also supports gpt-4-turbo, claude-3-opus, gemini-pro)
headline_results: Best system scores only 25% HMS overall
Reflexion (Oracle) + GPT-4o: 24.5% HMS on DB-REAL and 15.7% on DB-SYNTH; CodeGen, ReAct and DataVoyager between 5.7% and 16.3%
Per-domain (DB-REAL): biology 0%, engineering 7%, sociology 23%, economics 25%
Follow-up AutoSDT-Coder-32B raises HMS to 8.1 (17.4% relative gain) for an open-weight model
benchmark_features.holdout_or_split_design: DB-REAL: 25 train / 239 test tasks; DB-SYNTH: train/dev/test folders (repo). Metadata files bundle several queries per dataset (repo: 144 real-test metadata files hold the 239 test queries)
benchmark_features.leakage_or_contamination_risk: Gold hypotheses come from published papers, so LLMs may recall findings without analysing data; the paper includes a 'NoDataGuess' baseline that answers without opening the data to screen for such leakage
benchmark_features.primary_metric: Hypothesis Matching Score (HMS): LLM-judged alignment between predicted and gold hypotheses over context, variables and relationships, weighted by context F1
benchmark_features.sampling_strategy: DB-REAL: authors manually extracted discovery goals, gold hypotheses and workflows from published papers with public data (e.g. NLS incarceration/SES/BMI, World Bank education-GDP, archaeology, invasive-plant introduction pathways, meta-regression, requirements engineering); 114 tasks require multiple datasets (up to 6). DB-SYNTH: LLM-generated hypotheses/datasets/workflows with systematic variation of complexity (repo has synth train/dev/test folders such as ancient-languages_0_3, astronomy_1_2 encoding complexity levels)
benchmark_features.target_population: Real-world data-driven discovery tasks faced by researchers: from raw dataset(s) and a goal to a verified hypothesis, including data cleaning, statistical modelling and semantic interpretation

task_features.quantitative_tolerance: No numeric tolerance; hypotheses are compared semantically (context/variables/relationship) by an LLM judge, so quantitative effect sizes are only assessed insofar as the judge deems the relationship equivalent
task_taxonomy: workflow tags per task (e.g. time series analysis, data cleaning, data visualization, regression, meta-analysis)
six domains: sociology, biology, humanities, economics, engineering, meta-science
task_features.tool_composition: Agents iteratively write and execute Python analysis code (pandas/statsmodels-style) over CSVs, then verbalize a hypothesis; optional flags add domain knowledge or workflow tags to the prompt (repo: --add_domain_knowledge, --add_workflow_tags)

sample_environment_features.environment_description: Local Python execution with datasets on disk; metadata JSON supplies dataset descriptions, column descriptions, domain knowledge and queries; evaluation script compares predicted vs gold hypothesis (and optionally workflows)
sample_environment_features.novelty_control: Train/test split on tasks; synthetic tasks provide unseen domains and controlled complexity
sample_types: tabular CSV datasets from published studies (survey panels, economic indicators, archaeological artefact counts, pollen time series, meta-analysis tables) and LLM-synthesized tables
sample_environment_features.signal_quality_variation: Real datasets include raw and pre-processed variants (e.g. nls_raw vs nls_incarceration, meta_regression_raw vs meta_regression) so data-cleaning burden varies

tools: Reflexion self-reflection with oracle evaluator feedback

NoDataGuess control needed because published findings can be recalled without data

Small train split (25); no human baseline
Gold hypotheses reflect one paper's analysis choices; alternative valid analyses may be penalized

cards.summary: DiscoveryWorld is a turn-based 2D simulated environment (text/JSON observations with an optional 16x24-tile image) in which an agent must run complete cycles of scientific discovery -- form hypotheses, use virtual instruments to collect measurements, analyse data, and act on conclusions. It contains 120 benchmark tasks (8 discovery themes x 3 difficulty levels x 5 parametric seeds) plus 10 'small skills' unit tests, scored by binary task completion, a normalized procedural-progress scorecard, and LLM-judged recovery of explanatory knowledge. GPT-4o-based ReAct, Plan+Execute and Hypothesizer agents complete far fewer tasks than 11 human scientists (e.g. ReAct 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks vs. a 66% average human completion rate).

agents_evaluated: Hypothesizer (GPT-4o; explicit working memory of hypotheses and measurements, knowledge consolidation every 10 steps)
headline_results: Most performant agent (ReAct) completed only 38% of Easy tasks and 18% of Challenge tasks
Hypothesizer, best at knowledge discovery, recovered 34% of gold explanatory knowledge on Easy tasks and 8% on Challenge tasks
11 human scientists: 66% average task completion, 55% average knowledge score; 11 of 16 human-played tasks had completion rates above 60%
benchmark_features.holdout_or_split_design: Recommended theme-level split (train: Proteomics, Combinatorial Chemistry; dev: Archaeology, Reactor Lab; test: Plant Nutrients, Space Sick, Rocket Science, Lost in Translation); seeds >4 generate extra unvetted variations

instruments.name: Sampler, petri dish, counting computer, chemical dispenser, load cell, pendulum, rocket + launch monitor

benchmark_features.leakage_or_contamination_risk: Fictional scenarios with parametric variation limit memorization; the paper and README note the paper contains task 'spoilers'. GPT-4o is both the agent backbone and the knowledge judge.
benchmark_features.primary_metric: Task completion (binary completedSuccessfully), reported alongside procedural progress (scoreNormalized 0-1) and discovery-knowledge accuracy (critical yes/no questions judged with GPT-4o)
benchmark_features.repetitions_per_task: Official benchmarking runs each of the 24 theme x difficulty templates for seeds 0-4 (5 parametric variations) once per agent; Easy and unit tests capped at 100 steps, Normal/Challenge at 1000 steps (repo-verified, agents/README)
benchmark_features.sampling_strategy: Hand-designed by the authors: 8 discovery themes each with Easy/Normal/Challenge variants (24 templates); parametric generation (random seeds 0-4 vetted) varies object names, values and layouts. Paper suggests tasks 1-6 (Proteomics, Chemistry) for training, 7-12 (Archaeology, Reactor Lab) for dev, 13-24 (Plant Nutrients, Space Sick, Rocket Science, Translation) for test; unit tests all available for training (search-snippet)
benchmark_features.target_population: General scientific-discovery skills (hypothesis formation, experiment design, measurement, analysis) across diverse fictional-but-plausible topics, intended to test generality rather than task-specific solutions

task_features.quantitative_tolerance: Instrument readouts are numeric; task success is determined by scenario-specific scorecards (e.g. correct flag placement, correct nutrient chosen), not by numeric tolerance on agent-reported values. Knowledge is scored via binary critical questions.
task_taxonomy: Discovery themes: Proteomics; Combinatorial Chemistry; Archaeology Dating; Plant Nutrients; Reactor Lab; Lost in Translation; Space Sick; It's (not) Rocket Science!
Unit tests (Small Skills): Dialog; Pick and Place; Pick and Give; Instrument Measurement; Doors; Doors with Keys; Navigation in a House; Search; Discovery Feed; Moving Agents
task_features.tool_composition: 17 JSON action types (PICKUP, DROP, PUT, OPEN, CLOSE, ACTIVATE, DEACTIVATE, TALK, EAT, READ, USE, MOVE_DIRECTION, ROTATE_DIRECTION, TELEPORT_TO_LOCATION, TELEPORT_TO_OBJECT, DISCOVERY_FEED_GET_UPDATES, DISCOVERY_FEED_GET_POST_BY_ID) taking object UUIDs; instruments are used via USE(instrument, target); devices such as soil computers or crystal reactors are operated through dialog trees (repo-verified)

sample_environment_features.environment_description: Gym-like Python API (loadScenario / getAgentObservation / performAgentAction / tick). Observations are JSON dicts (nearby & accessible objects with UUIDs, inventory, location, dialog state, DiscoveryFeed posts, last action result, task description) plus optional base64 images with/without grid. Scorecards expose completion, normalized progress, sub-goal list and critical questions (hidden from the agent). A GUI (scripts/userstudy.py) supports human play; full world-state logs and videos are exported.
sample_environment_features.novelty_control: Fictional worlds; 5 vetted seeds per template; theme-level train/dev/test recommendation
sample_types: simulated soil, plants, rocks, artifacts, chemicals, animals/NPCs, reactor crystals, rocket components on a 32x32 tile grid
sample_environment_features.signal_quality_variation: Parametric seeds vary hidden ground-truth values (e.g. which species is the outlier, correct nutrient); no explicit sensor noise model documented

tools: environment actions only; Hypothesizer keeps a scientific working memory and consolidates it every 10 steps

transfer_relevant_findings: Large human-agent gap on the same tasks (66% vs <=38% completion) despite tasks being 'difficult but solvable' for domain experts
Procedural progress scores are much higher than completion, i.e. agents perform many correct steps but fail to close the discovery loop

Knowledge discovery lags task completion: agents can sometimes finish a task by brute force without articulating the explanatory mechanism (humans also did this, lowering their knowledge score to 55%)
Iterative plan decomposition (Plan+Execute) and explicit hypothesis memory (Hypothesizer) change the failure profile but do not close the gap

Repo errata: scorers for Lost in Translation and Rocket Science had bugs during the human study and were corrected post hoc; earlier knowledge scoring used a different scorecard key, so re-scoring released logs requires care
limitations: Single backbone (GPT-4o) for all baseline agents; costs capped per run
Only 5 seeds per template; some seeds >4 may generate unsolvable scenarios
Knowledge scoring depends on GPT-4o as judge over agent notes/thought strings
Simulated instruments return clean values; no noise, drift or calibration modelling
Human study covered 16 of the tasks (Normal/Challenge, seed 1) with 11 participants

Dimensionality of the parameter space (AF rises with dimension -- 'blessing of dimensionality')
Experiments-per-dimension budget (EF peaks at 10-20 experiments per dimension)

cards.name: Generalizability of Large Language Model-Based Agents: A Comprehensive Survey
cards.authors_short: Zhang et al. (Minxing Zhang, Yi Yang, Roy Xie, Bhuwan Dhingra, Shuyan Zhou, Jian Pei)
cards.summary: First comprehensive review of generalizability in LLM-based agents, defined as the ability to maintain consistent performance across varied instructions, tasks, environments and domains, especially beyond the agent's fine-tuning data. Situates generalizability within a hierarchical domain-task ontology, reviews datasets, evaluation dimensions and metrics (and their limitations), categorizes improvement methods (backbone LLM / agent components / their interactions), distinguishes generalizable frameworks from generalizable agents, and calls for standardized frameworks and variance- and cost-based metrics.
schema_axes_proposed: Generalization levels: instruction-level; task-level; environment-level; domain-level (hierarchical domain-task ontology; domains mapped to NAICS codes per secondary digest)
In-distribution vs beyond-fine-tuning-data performance
Variance-based metric (sigma): performance disparity across task categories within a domain (secondary digest)
Cost-based metric: 'generalizability cost' comparing specialist vs generalist agents (secondary digest)
Generalizable framework (prompting/RAG, no weight updates) vs generalizable agent (fine-tuned) distinction
Method locus: backbone LLM / agent components (perception, memory) / component interactions (tool selection, retrieval, re-planning)
Recommendation: standardized evaluation frameworks; dynamic curricula in low-latency sandboxes
transfer_relevant_findings: Provides the four-level vocabulary (instruction/task/environment/domain) for labelling what an instrument-control benchmark's held-out split actually tests.
Argues aggregate accuracy hides generalization gaps; recommends variance across task categories and cost of generality as reported metrics.
Framework-level generality (e.g. ReAct) does not imply agent-level generality -- benchmark records should distinguish the two.
limitations: Survey; no empirical validation. Detailed ontology/metric definitions rest on a secondary digest.

cards.name: Lost in Benchmarks? Rethinking Large Language Model Benchmarking with Item Response Theory
cards.authors_short: Zhou et al. (Hongli Zhou, Hui Huang, Ziqing Zhao, Lvyuan Han, Huicheng Wang, Kehai Chen, Muyun Yang, Wei Bao, Jian Dong, Bing Xu, Conghui Zhu, Hailong Cao, Tiejun Zhao)
cards.summary: Psychometric audit of LLM benchmarks motivated by leaderboard inconsistencies and poor separability among top models. Proposes PSN-IRT (Pseudo-Siamese Network for Item Response Theory), a 4-parameter IRT model trained end-to-end that jointly estimates model ability and per-item discrimination, difficulty, guessing rate and feasibility. Applied to 11 benchmarks (41,871 items, 12 LLMs via OpenCompass) it reveals varied measurement-quality shortcomings and shows that PSN-IRT-selected smaller item subsets align better with human preference.
schema_axes_proposed: Item discrimination (a): how well an item separates strong from weak models
Item difficulty (b): ability threshold for a correct answer
Guessing rate (c): probability of correct answer without competence (flags contamination/leakage)
Feasibility upper bound (d): max attainable success even for the best models
Model ability estimate (theta) as the latent quantity benchmarks should recover
Benchmark-level diagnostics: saturation / low discrimination, insufficient difficulty ceiling, leakage, cross-leaderboard ranking inconsistency, redundancy (item subsets can reproduce full rankings)
Human-preference alignment as external validity check for a benchmark

headline_results: Significant and varied measurement-quality shortcomings across 11 mainstream benchmarks

PSN-IRT-selected smaller benchmarks keep stronger alignment with human preference; third-party note reports Kendall tau = 1.00 vs full-benchmark ranking and 79.98% vs 72.11% response-prediction accuracy over classical IRT (unverified)
scientific_domains: general LLM benchmarks (e.g. MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval+)

transfer_relevant_findings: A benchmark schema should carry per-item difficulty and discrimination (or at least report their distribution) so that a 53-task instrument suite can be judged for saturation and redundancy.
High guessing rate is a contamination signal usable for physical-task benchmarks whose prompts leak online.
Fewer, well-discriminating items can preserve ranking -- relevant when physical experiments are expensive.
limitations: Requires a response matrix over many models; with few evaluated agents item parameters are unstable (see jiang_2026_trust_irt).

cards.name: Performance metrics to unleash the power of self-driving labs in chemistry and materials science
cards.authors_short: Volk & Abolhasani
cards.summary: Perspective arguing that SDL studies cannot be compared from publications alone because reported quantities (e.g. optimization rate) are not comparable across experimental spaces. Proposes a shared definition of an SDL ("automated experimental workflows (physical world) with algorithm-selected experimental parameters (digital world)") and seven performance metrics that every SDL paper should report, then reviews the literature under that lens (only 23% of surveyed studies included real-world benchmarking; 62% of ML studies showed model validation; 71% reported no precision data).
schema_axes_proposed: Degree of autonomy (levels: piecewise; semi-closed-loop; closed-loop; self-motivated)
Operational lifetime (demonstrated unassisted; demonstrated assisted; theoretical unassisted; theoretical assisted; plus labor requirements/scalability)
Throughput (theoretical throughput vs demonstrated throughput; covers material preparation rate and analysis speed)
Experimental precision (standard deviation of replicates of a single condition, collected in an unbiased/interleaved manner)

Material usage (safety, monetary cost, environmental impact: total active hazardous quantity; total material per experiment; high-value material per experiment; environmentally hazardous material per experiment incl. waste streams)
Accessible parameter space (demonstrated vs theoretical ranges; min/max bounds per parameter; parameterization in the optimizer; qualitative constraints on usable parameters)

Optimization efficiency (optimized feature achieved and number of experiments required; benchmark vs state-of-the-art literature and vs random sampling; regression validation with train/test split; explainable-AI parameter influence, e.g. Shapley plots)
transfer_relevant_findings: Autonomy should be reported as a discrete level defined by where humans touch the loop (data transfer, measurement collection, system reset, experiment selection), not as a binary 'autonomous' claim -- directly reusable as an agent-benchmark axis.
Report theoretical AND demonstrated values (throughput, lifetime, parameter space); the gap between them is itself informative.
Precision must be measured with unbiased replicates (alternate the test condition with random conditions) -- analogous to repeated-run variance for stochastic agents.
Optimization claims need a random-sampling control and out-of-sample regression validation; 'reaching an optimum' alone is not evidence of algorithm quality.
Material/hazard accounting per experiment is a cost axis absent from most agent benchmarks.
limitations: Perspective/heuristic; metrics are defined qualitatively, no reference implementation or scoring rubric.
Chemistry/materials focus; does not address LLM-agent-specific axes (tool use, abstention, provenance).
